```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE)
invisible(Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", "C.UTF-8"))  # keep non-ASCII symbols when built from a non-UTF-8 session
library(data.table)
A <- "docs/assets/isolaser_permutation"
est <- fread(file.path(A, "grid_estimates.tsv"))
pick <- fread(file.path(A, "selected_cutoffs.tsv"))
passing <- fread(file.path(A, "selected_cutoff_associations.tsv"))
focus <- fread(file.path(A, "focus_associations.tsv"))
perrow <- fread(file.path(A, "row_pvalue_summary.tsv"))
fmt <- function(n) format(n, big.mark=",", trim=TRUE)
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)
web <- est[cutoff == "|dPSI|>=0.10, het>=1, row p<=any"]
h <- focus[gene == "HNRNPK"]
```

isoLASER has no false discovery rate (FDR) control, so we estimated one by
permutation: shuffle which allele each read carries, score the shuffled data the
same way as the real data, and count how many associations pass by chance. This
pilot covers one chromosome and one timepoint, chr9 at 6 hours, where HNRNPK is
located.

**Result in brief.** The screen on the [genome-wide page](isolaser_genome_wide.html)
has an estimated FDR of about `r pct(web$sel_fdr_rows)` here: roughly 4 in 10 of
its hits would be expected by chance. Adding a requirement on each association's
own permutation p-value brings the estimate down to 4–8%, and an independent set
of permutations confirms it. HNRNPK passes every cutoff we tested.

# Why a permutation test

isoLASER labels an association `cis` when its score exceeds the 99th percentile
of a null distribution that ships with the software. That is a cutoff for each
test separately, not control of the FDR across many tests. isoLASER's p-values
can't be used for FDR control either: associations with no allele difference all
get p between 0.42 and 0.55, and the p-values sometimes contradict the `cis`
label. A permutation test builds the null distribution from our own data instead.

# How the permutation works

The question is: if a variant had no effect on splicing, how many associations
would still pass the screen?

| | In each shuffle |
|:--|:--|
| Shuffled | For each donor, gene and isoLASER phasing group, the haplotype labels (which parental chromosome a read came from) are randomly reassigned among the reads. A read whose label changes is given the other allele at every variant in that phasing group. The few reads without a haplotype label have their alleles shuffled at each variant. |
| Kept fixed | Each read's splicing status (whether its transcript includes or skips each exonic part), each donor's read depth, and which donors count as heterozygous for each association. |
| Broken | Only the link between allele and splicing. |
| Scored | Exactly as the real data: the heterozygous donors' 2×2 tables (allele × part included or excluded) are pooled and scored with isoLASER's own functions, then the same filters are applied. |

Two details matter:

- Shuffling haplotype labels, rather than each variant's alleles separately,
  keeps variants on the same haplotype consistent with each other, and keeps the
  exonic parts that share reads linked.
- Some shuffled tables end up with fewer than 10 reads on one allele and get no
  score; this happens for about 5.5% of shuffled values. They count as not
  passing.

## Starting from isoLASER's own read assignments

The shuffle has to use the alleles isoLASER itself assigned to each read, because
alleles read directly from the BAM files don't reproduce its counts exactly.
isoLASER doesn't save them, so we reran its per-donor step for chr9 at 6 hours
with a copy that records them. Before any permutation, we checked:

| Check | Result |
|:--|:--|
| The recording copy gives the same output as an unmodified copy run with the same random seed | identical, all 4 donors |
| Tables rebuilt from the recorded reads match isoLASER's counts | 23,214 of 23,214 variant tables |
| Scoring the recorded reads reproduces our heterozygous-donor results | 5,578 of 5,578 associations |
| The rerun passes the same associations as the original run | the same 20 associations |

isoLASER has two random steps, downsampling reads for very deep genes and the
starting point of phasing, so the rerun differs from the original run in a few
other associations, mostly in TPM2. The rerun is used for both the real and the
shuffled data.

# What we ran

All runs use chr9 at 6 hours, with `r fmt(perrow$tested_rows)` tested
associations (variant × exonic part with a scorable heterozygous-donor table).

| Batch | Permutations | Random seed | Used for | Run time (24 cores) |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|--:|
| Selection | 1,000 | 1 | choosing stricter cutoffs | 4 minutes |
| Validation | 1,000 | 2 | re-checking the chosen cutoffs | 4 minutes |
| HNRNPK focus | 100,000 | 3 | a precise p-value for HNRNPK's associations only | 16 minutes |

For a given cutoff, the estimated FDR is the average number of associations
passing in the shuffled datasets, divided by the number passing in the real data.
We calculate it separately for associations (variant × exonic part at this
timepoint) and for genes, since one gene can have several associations.

# Results

## The website's screen

The current screen (isoLASER `cis`, |ΔPSI| ≥ 0.10, at least one heterozygous
donor with ≥ 30 reads, part ≥ 10 bases, no clustered variants) passes
`r web$obs_rows` associations in `r web$obs_genes` genes.

| | Real data | Shuffled average | Shuffled, 95% range | Estimated FDR | Estimated FDR, validation |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Associations | `r web$obs_rows` | `r round(web$sel_null_rows, 1)` | `r web$sel_null_rows_95` | `r pct(web$sel_fdr_rows)` | `r pct(web$val_fdr_rows)` |
| Genes | `r web$obs_genes` | `r round(web$sel_null_genes, 1)` | `r web$sel_null_genes_95` | `r pct(web$sel_fdr_genes)` | `r pct(web$val_fdr_genes)` |

![Passing associations in each of the 1,000 selection-batch shuffles (grey) and in the real data (orange).](assets/isolaser_permutation/null_passing_rows.png)

## Stricter cutoffs

Before running these batches, we fixed a grid of 32 stricter cutoffs. Each adds
to the website screen a choice of:

- |ΔPSI| ≥ 0.10, 0.15, 0.20 or 0.30;
- at least 1 or 2 heterozygous donors;
- a maximum row p-value of 0.01, 0.003 or 0.001, or none.

The row p-value is our own addition: it compares an association's real score with
its own shuffled scores in the selection batch. p ≤ 0.001 means no shuffle scored
as high as the real data. It is what lowers the estimate most:

```{r row_p_effect}
x <- est[grepl("^\\|dPSI\\|>=0.10, het>=1", cutoff)]
x[, limit := sub(".*row p<=", "", cutoff)]
x <- x[match(c("any", "0.01", "0.003", "0.001"), limit)]
knitr::kable(data.table(`Row p-value limit` = c("none", "0.01", "0.003", "0.001"),
  `Associations passing` = x$obs_rows, `Shuffled average` = round(x$sel_null_rows, 2),
  `Estimated FDR` = pct(x$sel_fdr_rows), `Validation` = pct(x$val_fdr_rows)), align = "lrrrr")
```

This table keeps the website's |ΔPSI| ≥ 0.10 and at-least-one-donor requirements.

For each target, a rule fixed in advance picked the cutoff that keeps the most
real associations (or genes) while its selection-batch estimate stays at or below
the target. The validation batch then re-estimated each pick:

```{r picks}
pt <- pick[!is.na(cutoff)]
g <- passing[, .(genes = paste(sort(unique(gene)), collapse = ", ")), by = .(level, target)]
pt <- merge(pt, g, by = c("level", "target"), sort = FALSE)
pretty <- function(x) gsub("<=", " ≤ ", gsub(">=", " ≥ ", sub("het>=", "donors>=", sub("dPSI", "ΔPSI", x))))
knitr::kable(data.table(Target = paste0(round(100 * pt$target), "% of ", ifelse(pt$level == "rows", "associations", "genes")),
  Cutoff = pretty(pt$cutoff), Passing = pt$observed,
  Selection = pct(pt$fdr_selection), Validation = pct(pt$fdr_validation), Genes = pt$genes),
  align = "llrrrl")
```

*Passing* counts associations or genes in the real data, matching the target;
*Selection* and *Validation* are the estimated FDR in each batch. Every pick meets
its target in the validation batch.

The associations passing the 10% association-level cutoff:

```{r passing_rows}
p10 <- passing[level == "rows" & target == 0.10][order(gene, variant_qual)]
knitr::kable(data.table(Gene = p10$gene, Variant = p10$variant_qual, `Exonic part` = p10$exonic_part,
  `Heterozygous donors` = p10$n_het, Reads = p10$het_cov, `ΔPSI` = round(p10$dpsi, 3),
  `Row p-value` = signif(p10$p_grid, 2)), align = "lllrrrr")
```

*Reads* is the pooled number of heterozygous-donor reads; ΔPSI is the difference
in exclusion of the part between the reference and alternative alleles, as on the
[genome-wide page](isolaser_genome_wide.html). At the 10% gene-level cutoff,
C9orf72 also passes, with one heterozygous donor.

## HNRNPK

Both HNRNPK variants tested against the highlighted exonic part scored higher
than all 100,000 shuffles in the focus batch:

| Variant | Heterozygous donors | Reads | ΔPSI | Shuffles scoring as high | p-value |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| `r h$variant_qual` (highlighted) | `r h$n_het` | `r h$het_cov` | `r sub("-", "−", round(h$dpsi, 3))` | `r h$focus_ge` of `r fmt(h$focus_perms)` | 1 × 10⁻⁵ |
| chr9:83978398:G>C | 3 | 1,125 | −0.115 | 0 of 100,000 | 1 × 10⁻⁵ |

1 × 10⁻⁵ is the smallest p-value 100,000 shuffles can give. These p-values are
for HNRNPK only and are not adjusted for having chosen it. The two variants are
1.7 kb apart and may lie on the same haplotype, so they don't yet count as two
independent signals.

## P-values for every association

Each association also has a p-value from its own 2,000 shuffles (both batches).
After Benjamini–Hochberg correction across all `r fmt(perrow$tested_rows)` tested
associations, `r perrow$passing_with_q_lt_0.10` of the
`r perrow$website_passing` passing associations reach q < 0.10 and
`r perrow$passing_with_q_lt_0.05` reach q < 0.05. With 2,000 shuffles, no
p-value can be smaller than 1/2,001 ≈ 0.0005, which limits this correction; the
cutoff-based estimate above is the main result.

We did not pool shuffled scores across associations to make p-values. In an
earlier run, pooled p-values were wrong for individual associations: for 305
associations, more than 3% of their own shuffles had a pooled p-value below 0.01,
three times the expected rate.
